chapter_title: A Catechumen asked the Apostle: When I would give

spiritual_reading.full_translation:
This matter may be grasped by seeing the difference between harm that comes from hostility and correction that comes from care for restoration. When a will set against good first assaults another’s life and damages what should have remained whole, and then returns to press the harm further—renewing it and fixing it more deeply—what has been injured remains as a lasting trace. When this is brought before interior discernment, the one who has been harmed appeals to what judges justly within. Then that judging faculty examines the aggressor directly and searches out the quality of the damage that remains as a mark in the life, exposing the violence as though the very power of understanding had been split. The case is carried into spiritual judgement; a sentence is formed, and the evil is permitted to return into its own kind, so that the one who willed injury undergoes the measure he imposed. Because the assault was begun against one who had not first acted from such hostility, the condemnation is intensified according to the injustice of that beginning; and the opposition is not excused, because judgement follows the quality of enmity itself.

When this process has run its course, that hostile will is condemned for acting from retaliation and for setting itself in sin against another. Yet afterward the one who was harmed can still fall into a state of weakness, as the earlier damage opens into an active disorder in the life. In distress he turns to restoring wisdom and lays bare the disorder. That restoring wisdom holds no hatred and seeks no repayment; it applies keen truth to the corrupted state and makes a saving separation. In that work, interior life is released with force, and the person feels pain, yet accepts it because the end is healing. No injustice is in it, because the entire act is governed by good and not by evil as its direct aim.

When the work is completed, what was disordered is opened, what must be removed is let out, and the life is made sound. Gratitude and acknowledgement then follow, and the former distress together with the restoration becomes a testimony to the healer’s use, so that honour is given.

So it is with this whole matter in the presence of the living principle within a person: when truth first touches a disordered state it can feel like injury, yet it is good when it proceeds from the intention to set in order, and afterward it brings rest. From such restoration there arises glory for the healing work, even though the moment of correction is painful.

But there is also the opposite kind of action: one who attacks a companion in shared life from cruelty and envy of what is living, laying violent hands on the other’s state. Over such a will the accusation stands, because its impulse is enmity rather than the good of restoration.

paragraph_translations.translation: This matter is like the difference between hostile assault and just inward judgement. When a will set in enmity attacks another’s life first, it produces a fixed disorder and a lasting injury within what should have remained whole. Then it returns and presses the harm again, renewing the disorder and intensifying it so that the damage becomes a standing mark. The one who has been harmed then appeals to interior justice against the aggressor. The judging faculty examines the aggressor directly and searches out the quality of the injury that remains as a trace, exposing the violence as though the very power of understanding had been split. The case is brought into spiritual judgement; a sentence is formed, and punishment follows before the universal order that cannot be bribed. Retribution is permitted in the same kind as the harm: the evil returns into its own form, and the aggressor experiences the measure he imposed. Because he began the assault against one who had not yet acted from such hostility toward him, the condemnation is increased according to the injustice of that beginning. The opposition is not omitted, because judgement is according to the quality of enmity itself.
paragraph_translations.connection: DEVELOPS the principle of just judgement by contrasting repeated hostile injury with inward examination and retribution.
paragraph_translations.notes: Some phrases are textually rough (e.g., the quality being ‘as if he had split his head’); rendered as exposure of violence against understanding.

paragraph_translations.translation: After this reaches its end, the hostile will is condemned for retaliation and for sinning against the other. Yet the one who was struck can afterward fall again into weakness, as the prior injury opens into an active disorder in the life, and distress arises from that condition. He therefore turns to restoring wisdom and shows the disorder plainly. That restoring wisdom holds no hatred and seeks no repayment; it applies keen truth to the corrupted state and cuts it away. When this is done, interior life is released with force, and pain is felt; yet the person accepts it because he perceives the purpose. There is no retaliation in it and no injustice imposed, because the act is performed for healing. Everything done is governed by good as the end, not by evil as the direct intention.
paragraph_translations.connection: SHIFTS from hostile harm and retribution to restorative correction that can feel similar outwardly.
paragraph_translations.notes: ‘Knife’ and ‘blood’ resist literal spiritual phrasing; taken as keen separating truth and the forceful release of interior life in correction.

paragraph_translations.translation: When the restoring work is completed, the disorder is opened, what must be let out is released, and the life is made sound. Then gratitude is given and goodwill returns. The former distress together with the healing becomes a testimony to the healer’s skill, and honour is ascribed to the one who restored because the use is seen.
paragraph_translations.connection: CONTINUES the restorative sequence into completion, gratitude, and recognition of use.
paragraph_translations.notes: ‘Gifts and compliments’ generalized as gratitude and goodwill to keep the register spiritual.

paragraph_translations.translation: So it is with this whole matter as it stands before the living principle within a person. When truth first approaches a disordered state, it can seem like an assault; yet afterward, if the purpose is restoration, well-being is established and rest comes. From that restoration a glory arises for the healing work itself, even though in the moment of correction it is painful.
paragraph_translations.connection: DEVELOPS the teaching by applying the analogy directly to the soul’s experience of truth.
paragraph_translations.notes: The paragraph is fragmentary; supplied a continuous sense consistent with the surrounding argument.

paragraph_translations.translation: But there is also the other kind: one who acts upon a companion in shared life from cruelty, driven by envy against what is living. He lays violent control upon the other’s state, and the charge stands over him from enmity, because the impulse is to injure rather than to restore.
paragraph_translations.connection: SHIFTS to the opposite case, distinguishing cruel assault from corrective healing.
paragraph_translations.notes: The source wording is broken (‘comrade of the enemy’, ‘accusation of enmity’); rendered as a contrastive conclusion: cruelty/envious assault that remains under accusation.

spiritual_reading.overall_coherence: The chapter holds together strongly as a contrast between two outwardly similar actions—painful intervention versus hostile harm—distinguished by ruling intention (enmity vs restoration) and by the resulting judgement. Coherence weakens only where the source text becomes fragmentary in ¶7–¶8; even there, the governing opposition (healing truth vs cruel attack) remains clear.

findings.diagnosis: Coherent correspondential substrate: the teaching arises from the functional difference between (a) an enemy’s repeated assault that leaves a mark and triggers retributive judgement, and (b) a doctor’s cutting that hurts but heals. No foreign administrative taxonomy or jurisdictional listing intrudes.
findings.evidence: The chapter teaches by what actions DO: an enemy “hit[s]… make[s] a sore and a wound… [then] smites him again… [renews] blows” (¶4) versus a doctor who “takes the knife… and cuts this wound… the blood shall pour out… [but] did this thing… for healing” (¶5), completed in “heals it… gifts and compliments… honour” (¶6). The spiritual reading did not stumble here; it could map function-to-spiritual sense without forcing (enemy = hostile will; doctor = restoring wisdom). There are no named powers, ranks, watches, stations, or inventories; the ‘judge’ is part of the analogy’s function (discernment/retribution), not an administrative overlay.

findings.diagnosis: Genuine difficulty from damaged/fragmentary transmission, not a secondary administrative insertion. The paragraph is the expected applicative turn (“So it is…”) but key clauses are broken, forcing the spiritual reading to supply continuity.
findings.evidence: Text shows lacunae and unstable syntax: “This is also how this matter of [healing]… [It is] At the time ⟨p.238⟩ [when truth first approaches it,] it [seems as though] you have struck [it,]… [afterwards] ease… [and] A glory comes about… [thereafter] it exists [work of] it is painful [for the moment, though]” (¶7). The spiritual reading explicitly notes: “The paragraph is fragmentary; supplied a continuous sense.” This is a classic ‘application’ seam (analogy → soul) that belongs to the same correspondential teaching, but the copy is damaged enough that the reader must reconstruct.

findings.diagnosis: Genuine difficulty from corruption/fragmentation, yielding a clumsy contrastive coda. The intended contrast (cruel/envious assault vs healing correction) fits the chapter’s functional logic, but the surviving wording is too broken (“comrade of the [enemy]… sick with his [living soul]… accusation of [enmity]”) to read smoothly.
findings.evidence: Broken and internally tangled phrases: “Also, [this] is the other person [who] struck the comrade of the [enemy] sick with his [living soul, being]… he struck in [cruelty;]… according to [envy]… [he laid hands]… accusation of [enmity]” (¶8). The spiritual reading flags the same: “source wording is broken (‘comrade of the enemy’, ‘accusation of enmity’)… rendered as a contrastive conclusion.” Importantly, there is still no administrative voice marker (no jurisdictions, ranks, named rulers); the stumble is best explained by textual damage, not insertion.

textual_criticism.summary: 3 findings: (1) ¶4–¶6 is clean correspondential substrate with strong narrative/functional coherence; (2) ¶7 is damaged but remains the expected applicative turn; (3) ¶8 is damaged/corrupt yet still aims at the chapter’s core contrast. No administrative overlay blocks and no plausible insertion points requiring excision were identified. Recommendations: excise 0, annotate 0, none 3.
